solutions.check: 29 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Token pathetic gains by Labour at first

indicators.note: something pathetic is in a sorry, broken state, so these letters are knocked out of order
at first points to the opening letter of the word it follows

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged
the opening letter of the party name

explanation.surface: A political sneer: Labour's gains amount to no more than a pathetic token.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Token' reads as an adjective (token gains), but it is the definition as a noun: SIGNA from the jumble, then L.
explanation.definitionFit: A token and a signal are both outward marks or indications standing for something else, so the nouns are synonyms.

clue.text: Rumpus not out of place in parliament

indicators.note: letters that are out of place are not in their proper positions, so they get rearranged

blocks.note: a storm is an uproar or outcry
taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: An MP complains that a rowdy scene is not out of place in parliament.
explanation.walkthrough: Stormont is the seat of the Northern Ireland Assembly in Belfast, and by extension the assembly itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Stormont is the name used for Northern Ireland's devolved legislature, a specific example of a parliament.

clue.text: see 24dn.
More work by Ukraine's leader to dispatch President and one American

indicators.note: a leader goes in front, so only the opening letter of the country is kept

blocks.note: the opening letter of the country
taken as written
P is the standard abbreviation for President
the Roman numeral for one
A is a common abbreviation for American

explanation.surface: Ukraine's leader sends yet more work over to an American president.
explanation.walkthrough: 'More' looks like 'extra', but it is Sir Thomas More, author of the 1516 book UTOPIA; TO and P also make TOP, slang for kill, echoing 'dispatch'.
explanation.definitionFit: Utopia is the best-known book written by the Tudor statesman Thomas More, describing an ideal island society.

clue.text: Sol, beaten with ace (twice) blows a fuse

indicators.note: something beaten is knocked about and battered out of shape, so the letters are rearranged
to blow something is to lose or waste it, so a letter is thrown away

blocks.note: taken as written
the word written twice, with one of its A's then lost as the clue's end instructs

explanation.surface: A man called Sol, beaten twice by an ace serve, loses his temper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blows a fuse' is an idiom for losing one's temper, but it splits: 'blows a' drops an A from the fodder, and 'fuse' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To coalesce is to join or merge into a single whole, which is exactly what things do when they fuse together.

clue.text: Trial alternative? Put cards on table!

blocks.note: or is the word that introduces an alternative
to deal is to lay the cards out for the players

explanation.surface: An offer of a plea bargain as an alternative to going to trial: lay your cards on the table.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put cards on table' sounds like the idiom for being frank, but here it is literal dealing.
explanation.definitionFit: An ordeal is a painful experience that tests someone, and historically trial by ordeal was a form of judicial test.

clue.text: Determined to have good desperate try to rein in sex

indicators.note: a desperate attempt is wild and disordered, so the letters are thrown about
to rein something in is to hold it inside, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: G is the standard abbreviation for good
taken as written, then rearranged
it is a coy old word for sex or sex appeal

explanation.surface: Someone determined makes a good desperate attempt to control their sexual urges.
explanation.walkthrough: IT for sex is a crossword staple; the rearranged TRY becomes R...TY and holds it, after G.
explanation.definitionFit: Gritty describes someone showing grit, meaning courage and resolve, so it matches determined as an adjective.

clue.text: Cook did leg exercises to contain runs

indicators.note: exercises put the body through movements, so the letters are worked into new positions
to contain is to hold within, so one piece sits inside the other

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged
R is the cricket scoring abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: A cricketer called Cook did leg exercises to keep his run-scoring going.
explanation.walkthrough: Alastair Cook was an England cricket captain, which makes 'Cook' look like a name; it is the verb, the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To griddle food is to cook it on a griddle, a flat heated iron plate, so the verbs match.

clue.text: Flash oftener, it's said you'll get prison!

indicators.note: what is said is spoken, so the sound of the words counts rather than their spelling

blocks.note: to flash is to dart, and oftener is more

explanation.surface: A warning to a flasher that repeat offending will land him in jail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flash' suggests indecent exposure, but it means to move quickly; Dartmoor is a notorious old prison on the Devon moor of the same name.
explanation.definitionFit: HMP Dartmoor is a well-known British jail, so the name is a specific example of a prison.

clue.text: Fool doctors ruin orgasm after head disallowed

indicators.note: to doctor something is to tamper with it, so the letters are altered in order
the head is the first letter, and disallowing it means it is struck off

blocks.note: the word with its opening letter removed
taken as written

explanation.surface: A fool whose doctors ruin his sex life once his head is out of the picture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctors' looks like a plural noun, but it is a verb meaning tampers with.
explanation.definitionFit: An ignoramus is an ignorant or stupid person, so the noun serves as a synonym for a fool.

clue.text: Iris a major player in the rag trade?

definitions.note: the novelist's surname, identified by her first name

definitions.text: a major player in the rag trade

blocks.note: first meaning: the surname of a celebrated Anglo-Irish novelist and philosopher with this first name

blocks.clueFragment: a major player in the rag trade
blocks.note: second meaning: a media tycoon owning many tabloids, a rag being a newspaper

explanation.walkthrough: 'The rag trade' is slang for the clothing business, but a rag is also a scornful word for a newspaper, the tabloids being Rupert's trade.
explanation.definitionFit: Iris Murdoch was the novelist, and Rupert Murdoch owns many newspapers, disparagingly called rags, making him a huge figure in that business.

clue.text: Seed bananas plus energy

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bananas' sits among foods as fruit, but it is slang for crazy.
explanation.definitionFit: Pulses are the edible seeds of leguminous plants such as lentils, peas and beans.

clue.text: On back cover, 'Party substitute member'

blocks.note: a lid is a cover
a do is a party or celebration

explanation.surface: A book's back-cover blurb reading like a party list naming a stand-in member.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Member' suggests a club or party member; it is a euphemism for the penis.
explanation.definitionFit: A dildo is a sex toy standing in for a penis, and member is a coy euphemism for that organ.

clue.text: Practice vehicle all but covered in concrete

explanation.walkthrough: 'Concrete' looks like the building material but is the adjective meaning real rather than abstract.
explanation.definitionFit: A rehearsal is a practice performance run through before the real show, so the nouns are synonyms.

clue.text: Awful cover has nothing on Private Eye

explanation.walkthrough: This clue appears in Private Eye, so the magazine refers to itself as US, the way setters use ME for themselves.
explanation.definitionFit: Hideous means extremely ugly or dreadful, so it works as a stronger synonym for awful.

clue.text: Wilful dereliction seen to produce such Republican lie-spreaders

explanation.definitionFit: Election deniers are the Republicans who falsely insist the 2020 vote was rigged, spreading that untruth widely.

clue.text: Semen spilled – practised getting rid of a costume

explanation.walkthrough: 'Practised' reads as a verb but is the adjective meaning skilled, ABLE.
explanation.definitionFit: An ensemble is a complete outfit of coordinated clothes, the same thing as a costume.

clue.text: Offhand gent disposed of – what a surprise! – glamorous nightwear

indicators.note: whatever is disposed of is thrown away, so those letters are removed

taken as written, to be removed

explanation.walkthrough: 'Offhand gent' looks like a rude man, but 'offhand' is the whole word to cut GENT from. GEE is an American exclamation.
explanation.definitionFit: A negligee is a light, often sheer dressing gown worn by women, glamorous clothing for bed.

clue.text: Content, if stays tight

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.definitionFit: To content someone is to make them happy with what they have, which is to satisfy them.
